cleanIntro:
Chiappa publishes one manual for the whole Rhino line, and the 200DS is listed in its model table. The owner's part of the job is short by the maker's own rule: open the cylinder, unload, clean the bore and the six chambers, wipe the outside. The grip is the only part Chiappa says a shooter can safely take off, and only to oil the mechanism when it needs it. Everything past the grip, and any deeper cleaning, goes to a gunsmith.

One thing is different from every other revolver you may own: the Rhino's hammer is inside the frame. The hammer you can see is a lever that always springs back to rest, so it never tells you whether the gun is cocked. The red flag beside the rear sight does.

steps.title: Finger off, muzzle safe
steps.action: Before you touch the cylinder, take your finger off the trigger and out of the trigger guard and point the barrel somewhere safe. Chiappa asks for this every time the revolver is cleaned, handed over, carried or put away, not just when you think it might be loaded.
steps.prose: On a Rhino the barrel lines up with the bottom chamber, not the top one, so the muzzle sits lower in your hand than you may expect. Check where it is pointing, not where it feels like it is pointing.
steps.quote: When you inspect your revolver, you must first check for yourself to ensure that it is unloaded. Do this with your finger off the trigger and out of the trigger guard and keep the barrel of the firearm pointed in a safe direction.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — INSPECTION OF THE REVOLVER, printed p.28

steps.title: Look at the red flag, not the hammer
steps.action: Look and feel beside the rear sight on the left side of the frame. If the red flag is sticking out, the inner hammer is cocked and the revolver is ready to fire. The outside hammer will be sitting at rest either way, so it tells you nothing.
steps.prose: If the flag is out, decock before anything else, the way the book describes: thumb on the outside hammer and pull it fully back, press the trigger while you hold the hammer, then ease the hammer down as you let the trigger go. Afterwards the flag must be back inside the frame.
steps.quote: By the Rhino revolver a red flag on the left of the rear sight indicates, even by touch, the single action mode. Attention: when the flag is jutting out, the revolver is ready to fire.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — SAFETY FEATURES — Single Action Flag, printed p.25
steps.warn: Make sure that the flag is back into the frame and not jutting out.

steps.title: Lever down, cylinder out to the left
steps.action: Press the cylinder opening lever down and swing the cylinder out to the left of the frame. Hold it fully open while you work.
steps.prose: The lever pushes down, not forward. If the cylinder does not come out, stop and check the flag again before you force anything.
steps.quote: Press the cylinder opening lever downwards and swing and hold the cylinder fully to the left.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — UNLOADING, step 2, printed p.34

steps.title: Muzzle up, push the extractor rod
steps.action: Point the barrel up, still in a safe direction, and push the extractor rod through the cylinder so the cartridges or empty cases come out. If you shoot with a moon clip, the whole clip comes out with its cases.
steps.prose: Muzzle up lets the cases fall clear instead of hanging under the extractor. Chiappa supplies a small tube with the revolver for pushing cases out of a moon clip; do that away from the gun.
steps.quote: With the barrel pointing upward in a safe direction, press the extractor rod through the cylinder and remove all cartridges or casings from the cylinder.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — UNLOADING, step 3, printed p.34

steps.title: Count six, then look into every chamber
steps.action: Count what came out. There should be six, cartridges or cases. Then look into every chamber of the open cylinder and through the barrel to be sure nothing is left in either.
steps.prose: Counting catches the case that stuck. Looking catches the one you did not know was there.
steps.quote: Carefully count the cartridges or spent casings to be sure that you have recovered all of them. Make a visual check to be sure all charge holes (chambers) are empty.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — UNLOADING, step 4, printed p.34

steps.title: Field strip complete — the grip is as far as an owner goes
steps.action: With the cylinder open and empty, the revolver is ready to clean. Chiappa does not publish a field strip for the Rhino: the grip, held by one screw, is the only part it says a shooter can safely remove. Everything else comes apart at a gunsmith's bench.
steps.prose: Leave the grip on for a routine clean. It only comes off to oil the mechanism, and the book says to do that only when it is needed.
steps.quote: We recommend that you take your revolver to a professional gunsmith for disassembly and assembly. The only part which can be safely removed by a shooter is the grip, which can be disassembled and re-assembled through the relevant screw.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — DISASSEMBLY (FIELD STRIPPING) AND ASSEMBLY, printed p.35

steps.title: Bore from the chamber end only
steps.action: With the cylinder swung out, run the cleaning rod into the barrel from its rear, chamber end. Wet patch first and let the solvent soak a few minutes, then a dry patch to lift the loose fouling. Then a wet brush through the barrel a few times and a dry patch, and repeat brush and patch until the patch comes out clean.
steps.prose: From the chamber end is the maker's rule, and it protects the muzzle crown, which is what makes the gun accurate. Read the directions on the solvent you are using for how long to let it soak.
steps.quote: Warning: Always use a cleaning rod from the chamber end of the barrel.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — CLEANING, printed p.36

steps.title: Oil lightly, then dry it before you shoot
steps.action: Finish the bore with a light coat of oil. Before the revolver is fired again, run a dry patch through the barrel to take that oil back out.
steps.prose: Oil left standing in a bore raises pressure on the next shot. The book's safety rules make the same point: remove oil residue with a dry patch before shooting.
steps.quote: Lightly oil the barrel. NOTE: Run a dry patch through the barrel before firing to remove oil.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — CLEANING, step 6, printed p.36

steps.title: All six chambers, the same way
steps.action: With the cylinder open, clean each of the six chambers with the same routine as the bore: wet patch, dry patch, wet brush, dry patch until clean. Then dry the chambers with the brush.
steps.prose: Do every chamber, not just the ones that look dirty. Fouling at the front of a chamber is what makes cases stick when you push the extractor rod.
steps.quote: Open the cylinder and follow the same clearing procedure described above to clean all chamber
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — CLEANING, step 7, printed p.36

steps.title: Wipe the outside, dry it, store it
steps.action: Clean the outside of the revolver with a cloth and a little gun oil. Then dry the chambers with the brush, dry the outside, and put the revolver away somewhere safe.
steps.prose: A clean, dry outside is what keeps rust off the steel parts between uses. Do not leave oil standing on it.
steps.quote: Clean the revolver surface with a cloth and clearing oil.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — CLEANING, step 8, printed p.36
steps.warn: Do not leave oil residues when cleaning and lubricating your firearm.

steps.title: Oil the trigger mechanism only when it needs it
steps.action: This is not part of every clean. When the trigger mechanism does need oil, unscrew the Allen screw that holds the grip, take the grip off, and put standard gun oil into the hole on the top of the frame that the grip covers. Then put the grip back on with its screw.
steps.prose: This is the only oiling the book gives an owner. Cleaning the parts inside is a gunsmith's job, and for that Chiappa recommends a dry lubricant based on molybdenum disulfide.
steps.quote: In order to perform lubrication, unscrew the allen key fixing the grip, remove the grip and lubricate the hole on the top of the frame.
steps.cite: Rhino Revolver Safety & Instruction Manual — ABSENT — no revision, date code or edition statement is printed in the document. The publisher's file name carries the code 830.144; that is a file name, not a printed edition, and is not treated as one. — LUBRICATION, printed p.36
steps.warn: Do not use pure silicon or lanolin.

deepAbsentReason: The book stops at the grip. Chiappa's Rhino manual says the grip is the only part a shooter can safely remove, sends all other disassembly to a gunsmith, and says that for a deeper cleaning you should contact your local gunsmith (printed p.35). It publishes no deeper procedure for an owner.

cleaning.name: BORE
tasks: Rod in from the chamber end only, with the cylinder swung out
Wet patch and let it soak, then a dry patch
Wet brush and dry patch, repeated until the patch comes out clean
Light oil, then a dry patch before you fire again

cleaning.name: CHAMBERS
tasks: All six chambers, same routine as the bore
Dry the chambers with the brush when you are done

cleaning.name: OUTSIDE
tasks: Wipe the outside with a cloth and a little gun oil
Do not leave oil residue on the gun

cleaning.name: MECHANISM (ONLY WHEN NEEDED)
tasks: Standard gun oil into the hole on the top of the frame
Grip back on with its screw
Do not use pure silicone or lanolin
⛔ Nothing else comes apart — the inside of the gun is a gunsmith's job

reassembly: If you took the grip off to oil the mechanism, put it back on and tighten its screw.
Run a dry patch through the barrel and every chamber so no oil is left in them.
Swing the cylinder back into the frame until it locks.
Check the red flag beside the rear sight is inside the frame, then do the function check before you load.
fncheck: With the revolver empty and pointed somewhere safe, close the cylinder and check it is locked in the frame. Pull the outside hammer fully back: it should spring back to rest by itself, and the red flag beside the rear sight should stick out. Decock the way the book describes and check the flag goes back inside the frame. Work the cylinder open and closed a few times. Chiappa says the mechanism should move easily; if it starts to feel stiff, or anything feels or sounds different, do not shoot it and take it to a gunsmith.
